analysis.one_liner: Bans exporting pesticides the U.S. has banned or refused to approve, unless the buying country consents.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 97 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The United States bans some pesticides as too dangerous to use at home, but companies could legally sell them abroad — and those chemicals could come back to Americans on imported food, a problem known as the 'circle of poison.' This bill would have barred exporting pesticides whose registrations or food tolerances have been canceled, required labels in the buyer country's language, let the receiving country refuse or set conditions on shipments (with exceptions for disease and famine emergencies), and tightened monitoring of pesticide residues on imported food. It also let citizens sue exporters who violated the rules, with half of any penalty going to the plaintiff.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers and residents of countries that buy U.S. pesticides, who would no longer receive chemicals the EPA considers too dangerous for domestic use; foreign governments, which would get advance notice and the right to refuse or condition imports; and U.S. consumers, who eat imported produce, meat, poultry, and eggs that would face closer residue monitoring and disclosure of what pesticides were used on them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Foreign farmworkers and U.S. food consumers

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits exporting a pesticide if the registrations covering nearly all of its U.S. uses have been canceled, its food tolerances have been revoked, or the ingredient is ineligible for reregistration [S2][S3].

It requires export labels in the official language of the country of use and with the same health and safety information required on U.S. labels, and requires the EPA to notify the buying country before shipping hazardous or restricted pesticides so the country can refuse consent [S2][S3].

It tightens the link between U.S. pesticide cancellation decisions and food tolerances, and requires importers of produce, meat, poultry, and eggs to disclose which pesticides were used, strengthening FDA monitoring of residues on food Americans eat [S2][S3].
It creates a citizen enforcement right: any person can sue violators of the export rules in federal court, with half of any penalty paid to the person who brought the case [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers would lose the ability to sell domestically canceled or unregistered products abroad, a significant export market. Food importers would bear new paperwork and residue-testing obligations. Costs could ultimately show up in prices of imported foods and exported agricultural chemicals.

drawbacks.text: A blanket export ban could leave poor countries without tools against crop pests or disease vectors; the bill addresses this with EPA waivers for communicable-disease control and famine emergencies lasting up to 180 days, but critics could argue the process is slow and discretionary [S2][S3].

Export bans do not stop other countries from manufacturing or supplying the same chemicals; the bill tries to limit this by requiring a refusing country to certify it will not make or import the pesticide elsewhere, but enforcement depends on the foreign government's honesty [S3].

The bill layers new reporting, notification, and testing duties on EPA, FDA, USDA, and Customs at a time of limited budgets, and exporters and importers would face real compliance costs that could be passed to consumers [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health protections are real and targeted: chemicals judged too dangerous for U.S. fields would stop flowing to countries with weaker regulation, and Americans' own food imports would face better scrutiny. The main costs fall on pesticide exporters and importers, and the waivers for disease and famine emergencies blunt the strongest humanitarian objection. The main design risk is administrative complexity across several agencies rather than a flawed core idea.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat without a markup or a vote until the 102nd Congress ended and the bill expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Synar introduced the bill on April 24, 1991, with two dozen original cosponsors from both parties [S1][S3].
It was referred jointly to the Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs Committees, and within three weeks to three subcommittees [S5].

By mid-1992 it had 97 cosponsors — 87 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent — and had received an executive comment from the Justice Department, but no subcommittee or full committee ever acted on it [S4][S5].
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers kept their export market for domestically banned and unregistered chemicals, and food importers avoided new disclosure and testing requirements; consumers and foreign farmworkers got no protection.

for.name: Rep. Mike Synar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled two dozen original cosponsors spanning both parties [S1][S3].

against.name: House Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill at committee and subcommittee level for twenty months; no markup, no vote, no report [S5].

against.name: Pesticide manufacturers and exporters
against.role: Industry whose export sales of domestically banned chemicals the bill would end
against.what_they_did: The industry had long lobbied against 'circle of poison' export restrictions, which would cut off sales of chemicals barred from domestic use.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 87 of the 97 cosponsors were Democrats — but 9 Republicans and 1 Independent signed on, so the bill was bipartisan in sponsorship even though it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would ban exporting any pesticide whose domestic registrations or food tolerances have been canceled or revoked, closing off a market for chemicals too dangerous for U.S. use. Its interests ran against the public's interest in not exporting and re-importing hazardous residues.

Importers would have to file documents identifying every pesticide used on their commodities and run residue tests when unreported pesticides show up. The compliance cost serves the public's interest in safer imported food.

Growers could face new export documentation and limits on which chemicals they can obtain, but would also benefit from better controls over pesticide residues in the global food trade and U.S. efforts to build an international pesticide convention.
